abstract: Salmonella enterica is a zoonotic bacterium that not only causes serious economic losses to the livestock and poultry industries but also seriously endangers human health. Long-term indiscriminate use of antibiotics has led to drug resistance in Salmonella , and thus the identification of alternatives to antibiotics is crucial. In this study, the effects of puerarin on the S. enterica -infected chickens were investigated. A total of 360 chicks were randomly assigned as the control group ( CON ), the S. enterica group ( S ), and puerarin-treatment group ( P ). Chicks in the P group were fed the basal diet supplemented with 50 (P50), 100 (P100), 200 (P200), and 400 (P400) mg/kg puerarin, respectively. It was found that puerarin treatment markedly altered the serum activities of aspartate aminotransferase ( AST ), alanine transaminase ( ALT ), and superoxide dismutase ( SOD ), together with the malondialdehyde ( MDA ) and total antioxidant capacity ( T-AOC ) contents in the serum. The mRNA expression of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, Bcl-2, and caspase-8 in the livers of S. enterica -infected chicks was increased after infection but significantly reduced after treatment with puerarin. Histologic analysis showed that puerarin effectively mitigated morphological damage in the liver caused by S. enterica . Proteomic analysis revealed that S. enterica infection led to metabolic disorders in the liver, resulting in oxidative stress, increased inflammation, and significantly elevated levels of hepatocellular carcinoma biomarkers. The findings of the filtered sequencing were verified by using quantitative PCR ( qPCR ). Treatment with 100 mg/mL puerarin thus effectively alleviated disordered liver metabolism, reduced inflammation and oxidative damage and significantly reduced the levels of hepatocellular carcinoma biomarkers in the liver. The results suggest that puerarin has the potential to replace antibiotics to control Salmonella infection in poultry and thus improve food safety.

Animals and Experimental Design
All experiments were conducted in accordance with the Rules for the Administration of Laboratory Animals published by China's State Committee for Science and Technology. Two hundred twenty-one-day-old pathogen-free male White Leghorn chicks were purchased from Heze Xinhang Poultry Co., Ltd. (Heze, China) and weighed. + 200 mg/kg puerarin group (P200), and the
S. enterica
-infection+400 mg/kg puerarin group (P400). Each group contained 3 replicates. And each replicate contained 10 chicks that were used for sample collection and analysis. The CON and S groups were given a basic diet, whereas chicks in P50, P100, P200, and P400 groups were fed the basal diet supplemented with 50 mg/kg, 100 mg/kg, 200 mg/kg and 400 mg/kg body weight, respectively, of puerarin. The basal diets were developed according to the National Research Council standards (
Table 1

g

The livers were dissected and excised and rinsed slowly with PBS. A part of the liver tissue was fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde while the remaining part was stored at −80°C for proteomic analysis. HE

qPCR

The qPCR reaction condition were 95°C for 30 s (predenaturation); 95°C for 15 s, 58°C for 30 s, 70°C for 30 s (PCR reaction); and 70°C for 30 s (dissolution curve analysis), with a total of 40. The relative transcript levels of the target genes were calculated using the comparative 2
−ΔΔCt
method.

Protein Extraction and Proteomic Analysis
For proteomic analysis, the samples were divided into 3 groups (
n
= 3 per group), namely, the control group (CON),
S. enterica
-infection group (S), and the 100 mg/kg puerarin treatment group (P). Livers were collected and immediately stored at −80°C until extraction. Proteins were extracted in a lysis solution containing a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, Switzerland), 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate, and 8 M urea. The lysates were vibrated and ground 3 times, each for 40 s. The lysates were then centrifuged (15,000 rpm, 30 min, 4°C) after the lysis had been completed for 30 min on ice. The protein concentrations in the supernatants were measured using the BCA method.
Proteins (100 μg) were dissolved in triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer and 10 mM (tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine) was added and incubated for 60 min at 37°C. Iodoacetamide was added to a final concentration of 40 mM and allowed to react for 40 min at room temperature. This was followed by the addition of acetone, and the material was precipitated for 4 h at −20°C after which it was centrifuged at 10,000×
g
for 20 min and the precipitate collected.
Using an enzyme: protein mass ratio of 1:50, trypsin was added and incubated at 37°C overnight. Peptides were extracted using a vacuum pump. The sample was then completely dissolved in 100 mL of 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer and the peptides were desalinated and quantified. The peptides were dissolved in mass spectrometry loading buffer for LC-MS/MS analysis using an EASY-nLC 1200 system was used to separate the peptide samples. Thermo's Q-Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer with an MS scanning range of 350 to 1,300 m/z, data dependent acquisition (DDA) collection mode, and high energy collision dissociation (HCD) fragmentation mode was employed. The secondary mass spectrometry resolution was 17,500 with a primary resolution of 70,000. The differentially expressed proteins were identified using the criteria of FC > 1.5 or FC < 0.5, and a
P
value < 0.05. Functional analysis of the differentially expressed proteins was performed using gene ontology (
GO
) using Goatools and KEGG pathways analysis using Majorbio.

P
< 0.05.

INTRODUCTION
Both the poultry industry and public health are seriously threatened by the food-borne bacterium
Salmonella enterica
(
Knodler and Elfenbein, 2019
).
Salmonella enterica
is highly pathogenic to chicks less than 1-wk-old, and acute infection can result in death (
Patrick et al., 2004
). Infected meat and egg products can spread
S. enterica
through the food chain to humans, thereby endangering public health (
Guard-Peter, 2001
).
Salmonella
is a gram-negative bacterium and thus produces high levels of the endotoxin lipopolysaccharide in its cell walls which also contain pathogen-associated molecular patterns that trigger host inflammation (
Shah et al., 2012
). Infection with
Salmonella
usually results from oral intake, eventually leading to gut colonization and the rapid spread to internal organs including the liver, which in turn produces an inflammatory response (
Gast et al., 2021
).
Salmonella
infection usually induces a strong immune response involving the secretion of cytokines and chemokines, resulting in inflammatory damage (
Eckmann and Kagnoff, 2001
). During an infection,
Salmonella
is taken up by various cell types, including dendritic cells, epithelial cells, and macrophages, which frequently serve as the host's first line of defense against bacterial pathogens.
Salmonella
also depends on macrophages for nutrients for its rapid intracellular replication (
Leung and Finlay, 1991
). These nutrients include glucose, glycerol, fatty acids, and several other carbon-based compounds, allowing the pathogen to grow and cause systemic infection (
Thompson et al., 2018
). Studies have reported that during
Salmonella
infection, complex gut-liver interactions associated with the gut-liver axis contribute to liver injury, manifested by hepatocyte apoptosis, oxidative stress, inflammatory cell infiltration, and severe congestion (
Wei et al., 2019
). Abnormal levels of liver enzymes have been observed after
S. enterica
-induced enterocolitis in adults (
González-Quintela et al., 2004
). The liver has numerous important physiological functions, including the immune response, nutrient metabolism, and detoxification (
Nguyen et al., 2014
). Studies have found that the serum levels of alanine aminotransferase (
ALT
) and aspartate aminotransferase (
AST
) are increased after infection with
S. enterica
Typhimurium in mice (
Kalia et al., 2015
). In poultry, liver damage caused by
Salmonella
infection is relatively common. After infection with
Salmonella gallinarum
, the liver appears yellowish green, swollen, sticky, and brittle, accompanied by multifocal liver necroses (
Berchieri et al., 2001
).
Salmonella enterica
is currently resistant to several antibiotics. Therefore, the discovery of new and effective ways to combat
Salmonella
infection is an urgent task for the protection of both animal and human health.
Pueraria has been used in traditional Chinese medicine since ancient times. The flavonoid puerarin is the main active component of pueraria (
Guerra et al., 2000
) and has antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immune enhancement functions (
Zhang et al., 2011
). Puerarin can significantly inhibit liver injury caused by nickel in mice, seen in reductions in the activity of transaminase, as well as the inflammatory response, oxidative stress, and the levels of the pro-inflammatory factors TNF-α and IL-6 in the liver (
Liu et al., 2016
). In addition, puerarin can alleviate liver fibrosis through the TGF-β/ERK1/2 signaling pathway, suppressing hepatic stellate cell activation and excessive collagen deposition in liver fibrosis (
Li et al., 2019
). Furthermore, puerarin protects against CCl4-induced chronic liver injury, possibly through reducing CCl4-induced liver fibrosis by decreasing PARP-1 and, as a result, inhibiting NF-κB, the production of reactive oxygen species (
ROS
), and mitochondrial dysfunction (
Wang et al., 2016
). Puerarin can also mitigate non-alcoholic fatty liver in rats by controlling lipid buildup, oxidative stress, and inflammation (
Zhou et al., 2022
). In addition, in the zebrafish model of alcoholic liver injury, puerarin can regulate alcohol and lipid metabolism through the AMPKα-ACC signaling pathway, thereby alleviating hepatic steatosis and alcoholic liver injury (
Liu et al., 2021
). However, whether puerarin is able to alleviate liver damage in chick models is not yet known. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to investigate the mechanism by which puerarin influences
S. enterica
-induced liver damage. First, a model of
S. enterica
infection was established in chicks. Changes in the morphology of the liver tissue, serum biochemical indices, and the levels of inflammatory and apoptosis factors were observed, and proteomics was used to further study the changes in the liver proteome caused by
S. enterica
infection to determine the mechanism by which puerarin induces changes in liver function caused by
S. enterica
.

The secondary mass spectrometry resolution was 17,500 with a primary resolution of 70,000. The differentially expressed proteins were identified using the criteria of FC > 1.5 or FC < 0.5, and a
P
value < 0.05. Functional analysis of the differentially expressed proteins was performed using gene ontology (
GO
) using Goatools and KEGG pathways analysis using Majorbio.
Statistical Analysis
Data were analyzed with SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and are presented as mean ± SEM. Tukey's multiple comparison test and one-way ANOVA were used to examine group differences, and SigmaPlot 12.0 was used to create histograms. Differences between groups were considered significant if
P
< 0.05.

DISCUSSION
Salmonella
infection can cause liver damage through the complex gut-liver interactions in the gut-liver axis, which is manifested as hepatocyte apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cell infiltration (
Wei et al., 2019
). Puerarin is an active monomeric component of the traditional Chinese medicine pueraria that has been shown to be effective in alleviating liver injury (
Liu et al., 2021
). However, whether puerarin can alleviate liver injury in chicken models is unknown. In this study, we found that
S. enterica
infection caused liver damage in chickens which was effectively reduced by treatment with puerarin. Tissue injury increases the permeability of the hepatocyte plasma membrane, releasing ALT and AST into the blood (
Sala et al., 2001
). These enzyme levels are thus proportional to the number of injured liver cells (
Johnston, 1999
), allowing the prediction of the degree of liver damage by measuring the levels of ALT and AST in the blood. After
S. enterica
infection, it was found that the activities of ALT and AST, as markers of liver injury, were significantly increased, but decreased after treatment with puerarin. Cellular stress leads to the production of oxygen-free radicals, altering the redox state and leading to oxidative stress. Antioxidants can not only mitigate the detrimental effects of oxidative stress but also protect host tissues against immunopathologic damage (
Costantini and Møller, 2009
). In this study,
S. enterica
infection led to reduced activities of the antioxidant enzymes SOD and GSH-Px together with increased T-AOC and MDA contents, indicative of oxidative stress. This is consistent with previous research. Treatment with 100 mg/kg, 200 mg/kg, and 400 mg/kg puerarin significantly increased the T-AOC and SOD levels while reducing those of MDA. No significant effects were seen at the 50 mg/kg puerarin concentration. Puerarin intervention had no significant effect on the levels of GSH-Px. The results indicate that puerarin can effectively alleviate oxidative damage in chick liver caused by
S. enterica
infection.
It has been found that infection with
S. enterica
induces an immune response in chicks, leading to the overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, especially IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α (
Shen et al., 2016
). In this study, it was observed that the mRNA expression of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α was significantly increased after
S. enterica
infection, but was significantly reduced after puerarin treatment. Infection also significantly increased the mRNA expression of the apoptosis-associated genes Bcl-2 and caspase-8, although that of caspase-3 was not affected, an effect that was reduced after puerarin treatment. HE staining indicated the presence of severe liver damage after infection, with loose and irregular liver cord arrangement, damaged lobular structures, unclear boundaries, and large areas of vacuolar degeneration, together with the presence of Disse cavities and local inflammatory cell infiltration. Puerarin intervention could significantly reduce the damage caused by
S. enterica
to hepatocytes, and the effect of puerarin at the 100 mg/kg concentration was the most significant. The liver plays an essential role in the maintenance of metabolic homeostasis, and regulates both protein and lipid metabolism. In this study, we investigated protein changes induced by
S. enterica
infection and puerarin intervention. The functions of the DEPs were analyzed by GO and KEGG enrichment and a PPI network was established using the STRING database. According to the results of proteomic sequencing and related studies, key pathways were selected as the focus of analysis.
The expression of RAB20, TUBB1, and CTSV in the phagosomal pathway was significantly up-regulated after infection with
S. enterica
. In addition to the role of intracellular transport, Rab proteins also play a role in tumor cell proliferation, invasiveness, and drug resistance. Abnormal expression of Rab proteins influences the development and metastasis of cancer (
Recchi and Seabra, 2012
). RAB20, a member of the RAS GTPase oncogene family, plays a key role in membrane transport in epithelial cells and is overexpressed in several cancers, where it is associated with poor prognosis, tumorigenesis, and genomic instability (
Stenmark, 2009
). Cathepsin V is a lysosomal cysteine protease belonging to the peptidase C1 family (
Chazeirat et al., 2021
), which is highly expressed in various cancers and has been associated with cancer invasion and metastasis (
Gocheva and Joyce, 2007
). In addition, CTSV is also highly expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (
Jing et al., 2018
). TUBB1 is a key component of cytoskeletal microtubules and is involved in important life processes such as cytoskeletal construction, cell contraction, and mitosis. Compared with normal cells, tumor cells show more frequent mitoses and maintain higher concentrations of TUBB1. Studies have shown that TUBB1 is a potential therapeutic target for hepatocellular carcinoma (
Tian et al., 2023
). The expression of RAB20, TUBB1, and CTSV in the livers of chickens infected with
S. enterica
was significantly upregulated, suggesting the potential for cancer development, whereas the expression of the 3 proteins was significantly down-regulated after puerarin intervention, suggesting that puerarin may be effective for preventing tumorigenesis.
Lysosomes are organelles that contain hydrolases that break down dysfunctional organelles and aid in pathogen defense (
Régnier et al., 1997
). Arylsulfatase K is a member of the sulfatase family in lysosomes, and abnormal expression of ARSK can lead to lysosomal storage disorders, developmental abnormalities, or cancer (
Wiegmann et al., 2013
). ATP-binding box (
ABC
) transporters are the largest membrane protein family, and ABCB6, in particular, is responsible for the transport of various substrates in the cell membrane. Studies have reported that ABCB6 is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma, and ABCB6 has become a potential therapeutic target for this disease (
Zhang et al., 2020
). Here, it was found that the expression of ABCB6, ARSK, and CTSV in the lysosomal pathway in the livers of chickens infected with
S. enterica
was significantly up-regulated, which further suggested that
S. enterica
could cause hepatocytes to become cancerous. The expression of ABCB6 and ARSK was significantly downregulated after puerarin intervention, which further indicated that puerarin could prevent hepatocytes from becoming cancerous. This is consistent with the phagosome results.
An important biological process involved in metabolism is amino acid metabolism which is concentrated in the liver. Glutamate pyruvate transaminase 2 (
GPT2
) catalyzes the reversible transamination reaction between alanine and 2-oxy gluconate to form pyruvate and glutamic acid. While the GPT2 concentration in the body is normally very low, damage to liver cells increases the permeability of the cell membrane, allowing the release of large amounts of GPT2. Clinically, increased peripheral levels of ALT are seen in various types of hepatitis and liver cancer, and increases in GPT are also a sign of liver cancer (
Ji et al., 2023
). Copper-containing amine oxidases (
AOCs
) can catalyze the oxidative deamination of exogenous and endogenous primary amines (e.g., produced by sarcosine, creatinine, and epinephrine), generating aldehydes, ammonia, and H
2
O
2
(
Lyles, 1996
). These products stimulate the production of NF-κB-dependent chemokines and the expression of adhesion molecules in liver endothelial cells, and they may also initiate and perpetuate oxidative stress after the conversion of H
2
O
2
to hydroxyl radicals, resulting in inflammation (
Lalor et al., 2007
). According to research, AOC3-knockout mice are protected against the development of severe steatohepatitis and fibrosis (
Weston et al., 2015
). AOC1 also catalyzes polyamine deamination. AOC1 is recognized as an oncogene in both human gastric cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma, where it promotes cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by influencing the IL-6/JAK/STAT3 pathway (
Ding et al., 2021
). The expression of GPT2, AOC3, and AOC1 in amino acid metabolism-associated pathways in the liver of chicks infected with
S. enterica
was significantly upregulated, suggesting that the infection leads to oxidative stress in the liver, together with inflammation. The expression of GPT2, AOC3, and AOC1 was found to be significantly down-regulated after puerarin intervention, indicating that puerarin can reduce liver inflammation and alleviate oxidative damage.
Both steroid hormone biosynthesis and linoleic acid metabolism belong to the biological processes of lipid metabolism. UDP-glucuronidyltransferase 1A1 (
UGT1A1
) is the only metabolic enzyme that can metabolize bilirubin, which is a toxic pigment produced by the catabolism of heme which is mainly detoxified in the liver. The expression of UGT1A1 in the liver of the chicks infected with
S. enterica
was significantly increased, indicating that the bilirubin content in the liver was increased, but was significantly decreased after puerarin intervention, indicating that puerarin reduced bilirubin levels in the liver. The cytochrome 450 (CYP450) superfamily contains a variety of isoenzymes containing ferrous hemoglobin, which can play a role in oxidative metabolism in vivo. CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 are key enzymes that regulate bile acid metabolism. The expression of both CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 in the liver of chickens infected with
S. enterica
was significantly upregulated, indicating that the infection increased the concentrations of bile acids, leading to inflammation, with increased expression of CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 accelerating bile acid metabolism. After puerarin treatment, the expression of CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 were significantly downregulated, indicating that puerarin reduced the concentrations of bile acids, which could regulate bile acid metabolism and then lipid metabolism.
Pyridoxine 5′-phosphate oxidase (
PNPO
) plays a crucial role in vitamin B6 metabolism. Previous research has demonstrated that vitamin B6 deficiency can reduce the immune response (
Doke et al., 1997
). Vitamin B6 deficiency also affects the total numbers and proportions of lymphocytes, the mitotic response of peripheral blood lymphocytes to mitogens, and the production of interleukin 2 (
Meydani et al., 1991
), PNPO expression is also markedly elevated in most cancers (
Zhang et al., 2022
). The liver is the most important organ for uric acid synthesis. Excessive uric acid production can lead to metabolic problems. Xanthine dehydrogenase (
XDH
) plays a major role in the generation of uric acid in the liver (
Wu et al., 2022
). Additionally, XDH can oxidize a range of exogenous and endogenous molecules to produce ROS, toxic chemicals, and anticancer medicines (
Pritsos and Gustafson, 1994
). Studies have revealed that XDH-derived ROS can induce mutations, cytotoxicity, accelerate tumor growth, and cause endothelial dysfunction (
Battelli et al., 2016
). The activation of the caspase promoter is triggered by ROS buildup and promotes binding between receptors of the Fas and tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (
TNFR1
) families to their respective ligands. Cell death is caused by the activation of caspase-3, caspase-8, downstream BAX expression, mitochondrial cytochrome c release, and other factors (
Fulda and Debatin, 2006
). Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (
PSAT1
) regulates the serine synthesis pathway (SSP). The production of important enzymes such as PSAT1 can greatly enhance the concentration of serine and its downstream products (
Yang et al., 2017
). The overexpression of PSAT1 can block the formation of autophagosomes, resulting in the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and cellular material and leading to apoptosis (
Jiang et al., 2020
). In this study, DEPs such as PNPO, XDH, and PSAT1 were enriched and significantly increased in the Vitamin B6 metabolic pathway, suggesting that
S. enterica
infection could affect the immune system of chicks, lead to disordered uric acid metabolism in the liver, induce inflammation, and the apoptosis of hepatocytes. The expression levels of PNPO, XDH, and PSAT1 decreased significantly after puerarin intervention, suggesting that puerarin has anti-inflammatory and immune functions.
CONCLUSIONS
To sum up, this study first established a
S. enterica
-infected chick model. A puerarin dose of 100 mg/kg was found to have the best effect, offering protection against, infection and improving liver morphology, antioxidant capacity, and inflammatory indices in chicks. The results showed that puerarin has the potential to replace antibiotics to control
S. enterica
infection in poultry production and improve food safety. Analysis of the proteomic results showed that
S. enterica
infection led to metabolic disorders in the liver, leading to oxidative stress, induced inflammation, and oxidative damage, and significantly increased the levels of hepatocellular carcinoma biomarkers chick livers. Treatment with 100 mg/mL puerarin could effectively alleviate liver metabolic disorders, reduce inflammation and oxidative damage, and significantly reduce the levels of hepatocellular carcinoma biomarkers in the liver. The results show that puerarin has the potential to replace antibiotics to control
S. enterica
infection in poultry and improve food safety.
